builder_plan.scenario: An agent reads external documents or tool responses that may contain malicious instructions.
builder_plan.change: Replay attacks and legitimate lookalikes in an isolated copy of your agent workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your existing checks with the same tasks, permissions, and tool responses.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful attacks missed, legitimate actions blocked, detection delay, and review cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
summary: Tether replaces LLM-based monitors and stateless policy layers with runtime enforcement of formally verified stateful policies, inferred from system calls observed while executing each proposed action in an ephemeral sandbox. It costs per-action sandbox execution overhead and latency, requires writing and maintaining policies in an embedded Lean 4 DSL, and adds significant systems-integration complexity around syscall tracing. It can fail on attacks outside the modeled side-effect scope, on over- or under-permissive policy specifications, and when sandboxing is impractical for actions needing real environment state.
rationale: Runtime enforcement of verified stateful policies addresses real production risks of tool-executing agents, but the Lean 4 policy DSL, ephemeral sandboxing per action, and syscall-level instrumentation demand validation of latency, engineering effort, and coverage on the reader's own workloads before adoption.
technique: Verified stateful policy enforcement via sandboxed syscall observation

claims.statement: Tether replaces LLM-based monitors and stateless policy layers with runtime enforcement of formally verified stateful policies, inferred from system calls observed while executing each proposed action in an ephemeral sandbox. It costs per-action sandbox execution overhead and latency, requires writing and maintaining policies in an embedded Lean 4 DSL, and adds significant systems-integration complexity around syscall tracing. It can fail on attacks outside the modeled side-effect scope, on over- or under-permissive policy specifications, and when sandboxing is impractical for actions needing real environment state.
With a single shared policy, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while keeping the benign false-positive rate under 5% on realistic coding-agent benchmarks.
